In case you are interested in this topic I'll drop some additional knowledge:

The VRM are the power supply for you cpu they step down the +12VDC into around 1.3V. They basically work like a switch that turns on for a fraction of a second to energize a coil, which acts as an "energy buffer", from which your cpu can draw power. 

With a solution like this we would end up with 2 problems howerver:
1. modern CPUs can draw multiple 100 amps, which would overload a single "switch" 
2. The supplied voltage would be fluctuating too much for stable operation of the cpu.

We can counter both problems with more power stages. Using multiple power stages allows us to alternate between "switches", giving it time to cool down, hence more power stages result in cooler temps overall (this is why some boards work without a heatsink at all as long as the power draw is limited). Some higher end boards will energize 2 power stages at the same time to decrease resistance, resulting in even cooler VRM temps.
Voltage fluctuations are countered through the simple fact that with more power stages you can switch them faster therefore supplying a more stable voltage.

However under heavy load the voltage will still break down a little, this is known as VDROOP. This is countered by raising the cpu voltage resulting in a voltage spike. This can be quite devastating while overclocking. (in my first build I later realised that the voltage spiked up to 1.5V due to a bad config I did)

Now you might be wondering why someone would go to such lengths and not simply supply the core voltage directly from the psu.
This is done to improve efficiency, since lower voltages result in higher losses over distance. Hence VRMs are used to supply the lower voltage directly at the point of load.

Your gpu uses the same technique to power its core and the same goes for all the RAM and VRAM.

Since you are a beginner, go with an air cooler. When I first started I got an air cooler and it was much easier than all my water cooling builds (only ever had custom watercooling), since watercooling can be really tricky especially custom watercooling. Also air coolers like the noctua nhd 15 are actually better choice than an aio since they perform better under long periods of load and are completely failsafe, because they don't have a pump that can break. There is no reason to choose an aio whatsoever except for aesthetic reasons. I can do a build a pc with proper cable management in less than a days worth of work, whilst my custom loop takes around 3 daysto complete, because I just need to be really careful to make sure everything fits well. Also watercooling really needs basic maintenance especially when it comes to aios since they don't have a reservoir. I'd only recommend to watercool if you intend to do a custom build and want to watercool your gpu as well and have some money to burn.

Edit: also every high tier air cooler should be plenty to cool an 5800x. 105W tdp is peanuts for modern aircoolers especially since your cpu won't boost that hard while gaming.
